briefs.topic: Starship + global launch capacity trajectory 2015-2036: flights/yr, tonnes-to-LEO, $/kg, learning rates, and realized-vs-projected base rates for the space module of the AI-transition systems model
key_numbers: Global payload upmass (McDowell planet4589 annual reports, payload mass only, consistent methodology): 2016 338t, 2017 392t, 2018 389t, 2019 384t, 2020 565t, 2021 790t, 2022 1,029t, 2023 1,479t, 2024 2,541t, 2025 3,193t

2025 upmass split: USA 2,712t (85%), China 316t (10%), Russia 61t; SpaceX alone was 83% of ALL global upmass and 97% of US upmass (Q3-2025); 2,035t of 2025's total was business/commercial class (mostly Starlink)

Orbital launch attempts (McDowell): 2018 114, 2019 102, 2020 114, 2021 146, 2022 186, 2023 223, 2024 263, 2025 329 (321 reached orbit) = 16.3%/yr count growth vs 28%/yr mass growth (vehicles getting bigger)

SpaceX Falcon family annual launches: 2020 26, 2021 31, 2022 61, 2023 96, 2024 134, 2025 165 (~2,200-2,400t); 2026 target 170; max single-year multiple was 1.97x (2021-2022) — comfortably under your 2.5x WWII cap

China 2025: 93 launch attempts (record, vs 68 in 2024), 69 Long March + rest commercial (Landspace Zhuque-3 reusable methalox debuted 2025); but only ~316t upmass — China launches ~28% of world flights but ~10% of mass

Starship realized cadence: 2025 = 5 flights (F7,F8,F9 = 3 V2 failures/marginal, F10 Aug 26 and F11 Oct 13 successful V2 near-orbital); 2026 through July = 2 flights (F12 May 22: V3 debut, suborbital validation, splashdown success; F13 Jul 24: deployed first 20 Starlink V3 sats ~35-40t on near-orbital trajectory, ship landed, booster landing burn failed). Starship has still NEVER flown a full orbital insertion as of Jul 2026

Starlink V3: 1,760-2,000 kg each, 7m long, Starship-only (won't fit F9 5.2m fairing); SpaceX claims up to 60/flight (~106-120t); demonstrated 20/flight. Starship fairing: 9m dia, ~1,100 m3 usable volume — payload density needed for 100-150t is 90-135 kg/m3, similar to F9 Starlink stacking ~120 kg/m3, so Starlink is roughly mass-volume balanced but most third-party payloads are volume-limited well before mass-limited (effective tonnes/flight < rated)

$/kg current: Falcon 9 list ~$70M = ~$3,000/kg max LEO (~$2,700 reused); SpaceX internal Starlink transfer price rumored $15-25M for 50-70t = $200-500/kg (unverified); Starship current all-in flight cost ~$90-100M+ per vehicle build = realized ~$2,500/kg at demonstrated 40t — NOT yet cheaper than F9 per kg

Wright-law learning rate for launch (PNAS Nexus 2026 experience-curve study): 21.2% cost decline per doubling of cumulative kg to orbit — steeper than steamships and comparable to early solar PV; central projection $1,600/kg industry average by 2030, $300/kg by 2040

Musk/SpaceX cost claims ladder: long-term $10-20/kg and $10M/flight (reiterated through 2025); May 2026 post-F12 revision: fully-reusable target 'somewhere between $100 and $200/kg' at 100+t payload; marginal cost floor estimates $3-5M/flight (propellant <$2M + ops $1-3M)

Cadence claims: Musk Feb 2026 'launch every hour within 3 years (maybe 4)'; 'thousands of flights/yr' via overseas sites; '1M tonnes/yr to orbit within 3 years'. FAA approvals as of 2026: Starbase ~every-other-week Starship cadence (25/yr envelope); SpaceX seeking overseas sites explicitly to break US regulatory cadence ceiling

Orbital compute mass budget (the coupling that matters for your power constraint): Starcloud early designs ~85 kg/kW; SpaceX proposed constellation ~10 kg/kW (100 kW/tonne); so 1 GW of orbital compute = 10,000-85,000 tonnes to LEO = 3x-27x TOTAL 2025 global upmass per GW. Google Suncatcher's own viability gate: launch must fall below $200/kg by 2035; Starcloud roadmap wants 5 GW (4km x 4km arrays) by 2035
Cumulative mass in orbit: 16,185t end-2025 (up from 7,431t end-2014) — cumulative doublings driving the Wright curve are now dominated by Starlink replacement mass
base_rates: Realized tonnes-to-orbit CAGR: 2016-2025 = 28.3%/yr; but NOT smooth — 2016-2019 was ~0%/yr (flat ~340-390t plateau), then 2019-2025 = 42%/yr once Starlink self-demand kicked in. Launch-count CAGR 2018-2025 only 16.3%/yr

Maximum observed single-year global upmass growth: 1.72x (2023-2024); maximum sustained 5-yr: ~1.41x/yr (2020-2025). A single vehicle program (F9) peaked at 1.97x/yr. Nothing in the historical record violates your 2.5x/yr WWII mobilization cap — it binds only in fantasy scenarios

2015-vintage projections vs realized: FAA 2015 commercial forecast and Euroconsult-class consensus projected roughly FLAT demand (~20-25 licensed US launches/yr, GEO comsat replacement market shrinking); realized 2025 was ~10x the 2015 forecast baseline. FAA itself now concedes licensed ops beat its HIGH forecast in 4 of last 5 years (2025: +12% above high case). Base rate lesson: forecasts anchored on exogenous demand missed the endogenous Starlink loop entirely — ~85% of all upmass growth 2019-2025 was SpaceX launching its own payloads

Starship schedule slip base rate: 2017 claim = orbital 2020, cargo Mars 2022; 2019 claim = operational 2021; realized = first sat deploy July 2026, still no full orbital insertion. Systematic slip factor ~3-5 years on 2-3 year horizons, while COST claims have been revised UP 10-20x ($10/kg -> $100-200/kg target)

Launch $/kg realized decline: ~$54,000/kg (Shuttle) -> ~$3,000/kg (F9 2020s) = ~95% over the reusability transition, but F9 list price has been FLAT ~$67-70M since 2016 (monopoly pricing; costs fell, prices didn't). Wright 21.2%/doubling operated on cost, not market price — model should carry a rent wedge exactly like your power-rents mechanic

Vehicle transition base rate: new heavy-lift takes ~4-6 years from first flight to dominant tonnage share (F9 2010 first flight -> 2017 majority of US upmass; Starship first flight 2023 -> plausible tonnage dominance 2027-2029)
FAA/regulatory cadence approvals have lagged hardware by 1-2 years consistently (Starbase 5/yr -> 25/yr took ~2 years of environmental review)
contested: Musk '1 million tonnes/yr to orbit within 3 years' — contested to the point of implausibility: that is 300x 2025 global upmass, requiring ~50%+ sustained growth for 15+ years or 8,000+ Starship flights/yr; treat as narrative, not calibration
Starship $10-20/kg long-run — contested; Musk himself moved the near-term target to $100-200/kg (May 2026); independent analysts cluster at $100-500/kg medium-term; realized today ~$2,500/kg

'60 Starlink V3 per flight' (SpaceX claim) vs 20 demonstrated; V3 sat mass reported variously 1,200kg / 1,760kg / 2,000kg across sources — Starship's true operational tonnes/flight not yet established

Starship V3 100-150t to LEO rating — not demonstrated; all 13 flights suborbital or marginal-orbital; F13's 'deployment' was on a near-orbital trajectory (McDowell assigns U-designations, not orbital)

PNAS 21.2% learning rate — sound historically but extrapolation is contested because the curve is now ~85% one company; authors themselves warn against overdependence on SpaceX/Starship for continuation
SpaceX internal $15-25M Starlink transfer price ($200-500/kg) — rumored/unverified, no audited figures; SPCX IPO disclosures (June 2026) are the first real test of these numbers

2,500t-in-2024 'global record' figures quoted in press vs McDowell 2,541t — consistent, but beware other series (BryceTech, Space-Track) that include upper-stage mass or count deployed-from-ISS differently; pick ONE series (McDowell payload-mass recommended) for the model
Starship 'operational late 2026 at $1,000/kg' (orbitalradar-class secondary sources) — optimistic; V3 is still in test-flight regime with a booster loss on F13

stocks: cumulative_mass_to_orbit_t (Wright-law state variable; 2026 init ~ cumulative since 2000 ≈ 25,000t, annual flow adds current-year upmass)
launch_capacity_t_per_yr (2026 init ~3,500-4,000t; effective = min(vehicle fleet x cadence x tonnes/flight, regulatory cadence ceiling))
starship_effective_cadence (flights/yr, 2026 init ~4-6; regulatory ceiling stock rising 25->100+/yr with 1-2yr approval lags)
orbital_compute_gw (init 0; inflow = upmass_allocated_to_compute / kg_per_kw; kg_per_kw its own improving stock: 85 -> 10 kg/kW over 2026-2035)
launch_cost_usd_per_kg (cost, not price: ~2,000 falling on 21.2%/doubling of cumulative_mass; separate price series = cost + monopoly rent wedge)
loops: R1 Wright loop: upmass flow -> cumulative mass doublings -> $/kg cost down -> more self-demand (Starlink + orbital compute) -> more upmass. Historically delivered 28%/yr; gate it on Starship orbital success (Bernoulli event ~2026-2027, p~0.85 by end-2027)

R2 Self-demand loop (the one 2015 forecasters missed): 85% of demand is the launcher's own constellation; demand never clears at market price — SpaceX expands until marginal Starlink/compute revenue = internal cost, not list price
B1 Regulatory cadence ceiling: FAA/site approvals lag hardware 1-2yr; binds Starship at 25/yr from Starbase until ~2028; overseas sites relax it late

B2 Volume constraint: effective tonnes/flight = min(mass_rating, volume x payload_density); third-party payloads ~40-60% of rated mass; only self-designed payloads (Starlink, compute sats) fly mass-optimal

B3 Orbital-compute mass sink: relieving 1 GW of the terrestrial power constraint costs 10,000-85,000t of launch — at 2030 projected capacity (~15-30 kt/yr in the central case) orbital compute can absorb ALL of it and still deliver <1-2 GW/yr; it is a 2032+ relief valve, not a 2020s one
B4 Vehicle-loss setback loop: each Starship failure (base rate ~30% per flight in test regime, falling) costs 3-9 months cadence — reproduces the 2025 pattern (3 failures, 5 flights)
couplings: orbital_compute_gw adds to compute_stock via the same (compute x algo_eff)^0.85 aggregate BUT bypasses the energized-GW power stock entirely — it is the ONLY endogenous mechanism in your model that can shave the power constraint, and it arrives too late (<2 GW cumulative before 2032 in central case) to change the ~95% power-binding result before the early 2030s; in the 2033-2036 tail it can clip power rents 10-25%

Gate B3 on launch_cost_usd_per_kg < 200 (Google's own Suncatcher threshold) — central Wright projection crosses $200/kg cost around 2031-2033, never crosses at market PRICE unless a second supplier (Zhuque-3/New Glenn class) breaks the rent wedge

SPCX watch position couples to: (a) Starship orbital-success gate, (b) realized 2026 Falcon cadence ~170 (on track), (c) Starlink V3 tonnage ramp, (d) lockup waterfall to Dec 9 2026 — F13's partial success (sats deployed, booster lost) is roughly valuation-neutral; full orbital insertion + booster recovery before the Dec lockup is the binary that matters

China stack coupling: China 93 launches but 316t (10% of mass) and no operational reusable heavy-lift until Zhuque-3 scales — Chinese orbital-compute relief of ITS power constraint lags the US by ~4-6 years; asymmetric relief favors US in the late-2030s compute race
WWII 2.5x cap: apply per-stock as designed; empirically global upmass max 1.72x/yr, so the cap only bites Starship-specific tonnage in its 2027-2029 ramp years — correct behavior, keep it

lessons_for_model: Model tonnage, not flights: launch counts grew 16%/yr while mass grew 28%/yr — the model's launch stock should be tonnes/yr with tonnes-per-flight as a rising multiplier, or it will understate capacity by 2x by 2032

Growth is regime-switched, not smooth: 0%/yr 2016-2019, 42%/yr 2019-2025. The switch was one actor generating its own demand. Implement launch growth as a two-regime process gated on Starship orbital success, not a constant CAGR — mirrors how your compute buildout already works

Costs fall on Wright's law but PRICES fall only with competition: keep a launch-rent wedge symmetric with your power-rents mechanic; the wedge collapses only if a credible second reusable heavy-lift exists (earliest ~2029-2031: New Glenn scaling or Zhuque-3 heavy)

Orbital compute CANNOT rescue the power constraint this decade: at 10-85 kg/kW, a single GW costs 3-27x the entire 2025 world upmass. Even the aggressive case delivers only ~1-5 GW cumulative by 2033 vs the tens-of-GW terrestrial shortfall your MC runs show. Your 'power never normalizes endogenously' finding survives the space module — space is a late-2030s tail-scenario rent-clipper, not a fix

Forecaster base rate cuts both ways: 2015 consensus missed 10x upside by ignoring endogenous demand, but Musk-vintage claims run 3-5yr late and 10-20x high on cost. Calibration: take realized CAGRs (28-42%), apply schedule-slip factor ~2x to any SpaceX forward claim, and cap $/kg optimism at the revised $100-200/kg target rather than $10/kg

The 2.5x WWII ceiling is validated by this domain: nothing in 70 years of spaceflight, including the fastest F9 ramp (1.97x), exceeded it — cite launch as supporting evidence for the ceiling's generality

Suggested MC parameterization for space module: P(Starship full orbital + reuse by end-2027) ~0.85; tonnes/yr 2030 central ~15-25kt (bear 8kt, bull 60kt); $/kg cost 2030 central ~$400-700 (Wright), price $700-1,200 (rent wedge); orbital compute GW 2033: bear 0.3, central 1-3, bull 8-12; first year orbital compute >5% of new compute additions: ~2034 central

briefs.topic: Orbital datacenter economics 2026: $/W in orbit vs terrestrial, the $/kg crossover vs interconnection-queue-burdened terrestrial, and realistic GW-in-orbit timelines
key_numbers: THE KEY NUMBER (crossover $/kg): three-tier answer. (a) ~$200/kg beats an UNCONSTRAINED terrestrial DC on energy cost alone — Google Suncatcher paper (arxiv 2511.19468): at $200/kg, launched-power cost ~$810/kW-yr vs terrestrial DC energy spend $570-3,000/kW-yr. (b) ~$500/kg is the structural breakeven vs QUEUE-CONSTRAINED terrestrial (McKinsey; Starcloud says Starcloud-3 economics 'only work at $500/kg') — queue burden = 5-7yr grid delay (Dominion/PJM ~7yr for 100MW), interconnection = 30-37% of project budget, behind-the-meter premium 20-40%, claimed forgone revenue ~$350M/MW over a 7-yr wait at ~$70M/MW-yr cloud rates. (c) SemiAnalysis full-TCO model (June 2026, semianalysis.com/space-dc-tco): even at ~$250/kg orbital stays 3.6x today ($8.64 vs $2.37/hr per B300 GPU; LCOC $10.91 vs $2.49), ~30% premium early-2030s, parity ~2040 base case — because launch is only one term; 5-yr vs 15-yr facility life + 20% redundancy dominate. Model synthesis: use breakeven_$/kg = ~$200 + f(terrestrial power rent), i.e. ~$500/kg at 2026-level queue rents, ~$150-200/kg if power normalizes.

Current launch prices 2026: Falcon 9 dedicated $1,400-2,900/kg; rideshare retail ~$7,000/kg (cited by Orbital's CEO admitting 'economics of launch don't quite work yet', theregister.com Apr 15 2026, target $10/kg). Starship projections: $250-600/kg early ops, ~$94/kg after 6 reuses, $13-19/kg at 70+ flights (vendor math, speculative). Starship cadence reality check: 1 test flight in H1 2026 vs 6-12 projected — the $/kg curve is running ~2yr late.

Capex per MW (2029-31 est, Luminix mid-2026 report): orbital $255-505M/MW all-in vs terrestrial $166-174M/MW incl IT — 1.5-3x premium. SemiAnalysis 2026 actuals: 30.5kW/16-B300 cluster = $3.1M space DC capex vs $382K terrestrial (8.1x on facility; launch $1.6M of the $3.1M). Terrestrial reference: ~$12-15M/MW DC construction, new power ~$2,500/kW; CCGT capex $2,157/kW 2025, +66% vs 2023.

Radiation penalty: consensus collapsed from feared 5-10x to 1.5-2x using shielded COTS silicon. Google Trillium TPU proton-beam test: HBM irregularities at 2 krad(Si) vs 750 rad expected shielded 5-yr dose (~3x margin); no hard failure to 15 krad. Shielding mass <2% cost at Starship economics (SemiAnalysis).

Refresh/depreciation: orbital 5-7yr whole-stack life (bus+solar+radiators die with sat; relaunch required) vs terrestrial 15-yr facility life — vs the model's 25%/yr terrestrial IT depreciation, the IT refresh is similar; the asymmetry is the FACILITY being consumable in orbit. SemiAnalysis assumes life extends to 10yr post-2032 via robotics. Redundancy: 20% spare GPUs in orbit vs 5% terrestrial. Availability 95% (solar events) vs ~100%.

Thermal/mass budget: ~1.4 m2 radiator per H100 (~700W), ~80 m2 per 40kW rack, +40% area after 5-yr surface degradation; ~2.5 kg/kW radiator mass; effective PUE ~1.3 vs 1.5-2.0 terrestrial. All-in mass intensity ~10-20 kg/kW (Starcloud-3 = 3t/200kW = 15 kg/kW; Google's $810/kW-yr at $200/kg implies ~20 kg/kW over 5yr). Solar in dawn-dusk SSO ~8x more productive per panel than ground, 60% (LEO) to ~97% (SSO) sunlight fraction.

Latency/bandwidth: LEO RTT 4.6-7.4ms (340-550km) — batch training and batch inference fine (~70-75% of GPU-hours claimed addressable: training 40-60%, batch inference 20-30%); real-time inference 20-30% incompatible. Intra-cluster: Google demoed 800Gbps/direction (1.6Tbps) per optical ISL pair, 100-200m sat spacing, needs 'tens of Tbps' for DC-scale ML. Ground-to-orbit data ingress is the unsolved link for big training runs.

Programs as of mid-2026: Starcloud — Starcloud-1 flew Nov 2025 (H100, ~1kW, first AI training in orbit), Starcloud-2 Oct 2026 (B200+H100s+AWS blade, 7kW, plus bitcoin ASICs as revenue bridge), Starcloud-3 3t/200kW, claims $0.05/kWh; $170M Series A at $1.1B (Mar 2026, NVIDIA-backed); FCC filing for 88,000 sats / ~20GW (paper). Google Suncatcher: 2 prototype sats w/ Planet by early 2027; in talks with SpaceX for launches (WSJ May 13 2026); 81-sat/1km-radius/650km cluster design. Axiom: ODC nodes 1-2 launched Jan 11 2026 (kW-class, on Kepler optical relay net), roadmap kW→MW. ESA/ASCEND (Thales-led, Horizon Europe): 1 GW target 'before 2050', small demo module 2026. China: Guoxing (ADA Space) 'Star Compute' 2,800 sats (2,400 inference/400 training); 'Prometheus' space-cloud platform launched Mar 2026 w/ MIIT; stated GW-level ambition.

GW-in-orbit timeline: 1 GW at 10-20 kg/kW = 10,000-20,000 t to LEO ≈ 50-100+ Starship flights (200t class) — 4-8x TOTAL world 2025 orbital upmass (~2,500 t/yr, mostly Starlink). 100 MW ≈ 50+ dedicated Starship missions at <$100/kg assumed 2029-31. Realistic first GW: mid-2030s (McKinsey). Market sizing: $1.8B 2029 → $39B 2035 (BIS Research, 67% CAGR). Feb 2026 = first month with multiple orbital DC operators running production workloads (all kW-scale).

Insurance/risk: no published premium structures yet; Lloyd's + ~25 insurers in exploratory talks June 2026; total space insurance market ~$500M/yr vs $300-500M hardware per orbital MW — a single-launch loss exceeds the whole market's annual premium pool; expected loss $6-10M/launch even at 98% reliability.
base_rates: Launch cost decline base rate: Shuttle ~$54,000/kg → Falcon 9 ~$1,400-2,700/kg over ~30yr (~20%/yr in the F9 decade, then a 2015-2025 PLATEAU — price fell far slower than cost; SpaceX monopoly kept margin). Assuming Wright's-law resumption requires Starship cadence; historical precedent is one step-change per ~15yr, not a smooth curve.

Constellation deployment base rate: Starlink 0 → ~7,000 sats and ~2,000-2,500 t/yr upmass in ~6 years — the fastest space buildout ever, and it consumed essentially all of SpaceX's marginal capacity. Orbital compute must compete with Starlink V3 for the same manifests.

Space infrastructure cost-overrun base rate: ISS = ~$150B for ~100 kW usable power (>$1M/W); every prior large space-power program missed cost targets by 5-50x. Current orbital DC estimates ($255-505/W) are already 250-500x better than ISS-era — treat vendor claims of further 10x as low-probability.

Demo-to-GW scaling base rate: offshore wind took ~20yr from first 5MW demo to first GW farm; nuclear ~15yr demo→GW; solar PV ~25yr. kW-scale orbital demos in 2026 → GW in orbit before 2034 would be the fastest energy-infrastructure scaling in history, above WWII rates.

Prediction-vs-outcome base rate for this exact sector: H1 2026 Starship flights predicted 6-12, actual 1. Orbital startup (Orbital Inc) publicly conceded economics don't work at current prices. Vendor $/kWh claims ($0.005-0.05) are 10-100x below what third-party TCO models compute today.
contested: Starcloud's $0.05/kWh orbital energy claim and $0.005/kWh space-solar cost — vendor numbers; SemiAnalysis third-party TCO puts today's all-in orbital compute at 3.6-4.4x terrestrial. Both cannot be right.

The $350M/MW 'forgone revenue' queue cost (Luminix) uses GROSS cloud revenue (~$70M/MW-yr), not margin, and assumes zero alternative siting — behind-the-meter gas (101 GW announced) is the real-world arbitrage and caps queue rents at a 20-40% capex premium, not $350M/MW. Using the gross figure makes orbital breakeven look ~2-3x easier than it is.

McKinsey ~$500/kg structural breakeven vs SemiAnalysis ~2040 parity even at $250/kg — these disagree materially; the difference is whether you count facility-life asymmetry and redundancy, or only energy+launch. Model both branches.

1.5-2x radiation premium 'consensus' rests on ONE proton-beam test (Google Trillium) + early NVIDIA commercial-node flights; HBM showed irregularities at 2 krad. Fleet-scale annual failure rates in orbit are unmeasured; the 5-10x bear case is wounded, not dead.
$13-19/kg mature-Starship and $10/kg Musk-target figures are aspirational; no third party prices Starship below ~$250/kg this decade. H1 2026 cadence (1 flight) argues for the slow branch.

'75% of AI workloads are latency-tolerant hence orbit-suitable' ignores data gravity: multi-Tbps ground↔orbit ingress for training corpora/checkpoints is undemonstrated (best demo 1.6Tbps per ISL pair, intra-cluster only).
Starcloud 88,000-sat/20GW FCC filing and 5GW/4km2 hypercluster are paper filings, not plans-of-record; FCC filings are cheap options. Similarly ESA's '1GW before 2050' is a study, not a program.

The Luminix 'Data Centers in Space' report (useluminix.com) is an AI-aggregator-style secondary source; its numbers cross-check well against SemiAnalysis/Google primaries but should not be cited as independent confirmation.

stocks: orbital_compute_gw — energized GW in orbit (starts ~0.00002 GW in 2026, i.e. tens of kW); adds to effective compute with 1.5-2x capex premium, PUE 1.3, 95% availability, training/batch-only (cap at ~70% of workload addressability)
launch_capacity_tons_per_yr — world LEO upmass capacity (base ~2,500 t/yr 2025); subject to the existing 2.5x/yr WWII mobilization ceiling; Starlink pre-empts a large fixed share

launch_cost_per_kg — declining state variable, Wright's law ~15-20% per doubling of cumulative Starship-class flights, floor ~$100-250/kg this horizon; plateaus if cadence stalls (H1-2026 evidence: stalled)
orbital_pipeline (optional, mirrors the 3-stage power pipeline): design→launch-manifest→commissioned, ~2-3yr lag, feeding orbital_compute_gw
loops: B1 power-relief loop: terrestrial power rent ↑ → orbital breakeven_$/kg ↑ (from ~$200 base toward ~$500+) → deployment gate opens sooner → orbital_compute_gw relieves power constraint — but sized so relief is <1-2 GW by 2036, i.e. it does NOT let power normalize endogenously (consistent with existing model behavior)

R1 launch learning loop: orbital + Starlink demand → cadence → Wright's-law $/kg decline → more orbital demand becomes economic → more launch demand. This is the SPCX reflexivity loop; it is currently stalled at the cadence link

B2 relaunch-drag loop: orbital stock × (1/5-7yr life) = recurring relaunch tonnage demand that consumes launch_capacity, throttling net growth (steady-state: ~15-20% of stock relaunched/yr, at 10-20 kg/kW)
B3 insurance/loss loop (weak): deployment scale ↑ → single-event exposure exceeds insurance market → uninsured builds → a loss event pauses deployment 1-2yr (stochastic shock candidate)
couplings: Gate: orbital deployment rate > 0 only when launch_cost_per_kg < breakeven_$/kg, where breakeven = $200 + k × power_rent_index (calibrate so 2026 queue conditions give ~$500/kg); this couples the space module directly to the existing power-rents machinery
Compute coupling: orbital GW enters compute_stock via the same (compute×algo_eff)^0.85 aggregate but with a 0.7 workload-addressability multiplier and 5-7yr (not 25%/yr) whole-stack depreciation

SPCX watch coupling: Starship cadence is the single upstream driver of launch_cost_per_kg; a cadence miss (observed H1 2026) shifts the orbital option ~2yr right; Google-SpaceX launch talks (May 2026) are a demand-side positive for SPCX independent of whether orbital DCs pencil — SpaceX gets paid either way (picks-and-shovels asymmetry relevant to the $1.52T post-lockup mark)

Mobilization-ceiling coupling: 1 GW orbital = 10-20 kt to LEO = 4-8x 2025 world upmass; under the 2.5x/yr ceiling off a 2,500 t/yr base (with Starlink pre-emption), first orbital GW is physically unreachable before ~2032 and plausible only 2034-2036 in the Starship-success branch — encode as hard feasibility check, not just economics

lessons_for_model: Orbital compute CANNOT rescue the power constraint on this model's horizon: even the optimist path yields 0.1-2 GW in orbit by 2036 vs hundreds of GW of terrestrial AI demand — <1% relief. Its correct role in the model is (a) an option-value term on terrestrial power rents post-2033 and (b) a ceiling on how far power rents can run in the very long term (rents can't exceed the orbital backstop cost forever), not a relief valve. This is consistent with power never normalizing endogenously in the existing runs.

Encode the crossover as a moving threshold, not a constant: breakeven_$/kg ≈ $200 (unconstrained parity, Google) rising to ~$500 (2026-level queue rents, McKinsey/Starcloud) — i.e., the power constraint the model already has is precisely what makes orbital investable. Current price $1,400-2,900/kg means the gate is 3-14x away; only the Starship branch closes it.

Launch tonnage is a second pipeline constraint structurally identical to the power pipeline: apply the existing 2.5x/yr mobilization ceiling to upmass (base 2,500 t/yr), subtract Starlink pre-emption, charge 10-20 kg/kW plus 15-20%/yr relaunch drag. The hard feasibility check (no GW before ~2032) should bind before economics does in most runs.

Depreciation asymmetry is the buried killer, not launch: SemiAnalysis shows 5-yr whole-stack orbital life vs 15-yr terrestrial facility life contributes more to the 3.6-4.4x TCO gap than $/kg does at Starship prices. Any run that gives orbital a win must also model robotic-servicing success (life →10yr post-2032) — treat as a separate low-probability switch.

SPCX watch implication: the orbital-DC narrative is a call option embedded in the $1.52T mark, but the H1 2026 cadence miss (1 flight vs 6-12 projected) is direct evidence against the near-term $/kg curve; meanwhile SpaceX monetizes the hype via launch contracts (Google talks, Starcloud manifests) regardless of whether orbital DCs ever pencil — asymmetric positive for launch revenue, negative for '20GW constellation' terminal-value stories inside the lockup-waterfall window to Dec 9 2026.

Radiation-premium update is genuinely bullish and should be reflected: 1.5-2x COTS-with-shielding (validated by Google beam tests, NVIDIA flights) replaces the 5-10x rad-hard prior — this moved the orbital cost curve more in 12 months than launch prices did. Keep a 20% Monte Carlo branch where fleet-scale HBM failures resurrect the bear case.

briefs.topic: Hard physics constraints on space-based compute: thermal/radiator mass, radiation on advanced-node silicon, debris/regulation, power beaming — which constraints scale away with cheap launch and which do not (feed for space module, task #23)
key_numbers: THERMAL (the real binding constraint): ISS ETCS benchmark = 70 kW rejected via 422 m2 ammonia-loop radiators massing ~7 t -> ~100 kg/kW and only ~166 W/m2 achieved in practice (vs Stefan-Boltzmann ideal ~430 W/m2 one-sided at 300 K, eps~0.9). Rule of thumb: ~2.5 m2 of radiator per kW near room temp; ~1,200-2,500 m2 per MW.

Radiator panel areal mass: conventional deployable panels 5-10 kg/m2 -> 12-25 kg/kW at datacenter-chip temperatures. A 100 MW orbital datacenter needs ~7,000 t of conventional radiator panels (~15 ISS masses). Sun-facing radiators absorb ~200 W/m2 solar+albedo, cutting net rejection roughly in half — orientation and dawn-dusk SSO orbits mitigate.

T^4 leverage: net flux ~418 W/m2/side at 20C, ~850 W/m2 at 80C (GPU coolant temp), ~1,450 W/m2 at 127C (electronics limit). Running chips hot is worth more than any radiator material advance, but AI silicon wants junction <105C, capping radiator temp ~50-80C.

Advanced radiators: liquid droplet radiators (LDR) demonstrated 450 W/kg (~2.2 kg/kW) in Nov-2025 Applied Thermal Engineering study; NASA 1980s work says up to 7x lighter than panels. Still developmental (TRL ~3-4 since the 1980s, never flown at scale). Counter-claim (Mach33): at 100 kW satellite scale radiators are only 10-20% of total mass — thermal dominance is scale- and temperature-dependent.

RADIATION (surprisingly NOT binding): Google Suncatcher paper (arXiv 2511.19468) — Trillium TPUs survived TID to 15 krad(Si) with no hard failures; most sensitive part is HBM, showing irregularities at 2 krad(Si) ~ 3x the expected 5-yr mission dose of 750 rad(Si) in dawn-dusk SSO behind shielding. LEO SSO dose ~150 rad(Si)/yr behind ~10 mm Al-equivalent. ~100 krad tolerance suffices for multi-year LEO. SEUs handled by ECC + checkpointing (single-digit-% throughput overhead), same discipline terrestrial 100k-GPU runs already need. South Atlantic Anomaly spikes SEU/SEL rates each pass.

POWER BEAMING (rules out separating generation from compute): microwave end-to-end DC-to-DC ~40-45% (DC-RF 69% x propagation 95% x RF-DC rectenna 79% x spot capture 87% = 44.8%); lasers worse through atmosphere. So space-solar->ground-compute pays a ~2.2x power penalty plus km-scale rectennas; co-locating compute with generation in orbit is the only architecture that pencils — which is exactly why 'datacenter in space' displaced 'space solar power' (50 yrs of SSP studies, zero deployments).

LAUNCH ECONOMICS: Falcon 9 today ~$2,800/kg price; Google learning-curve extrapolation -> <$200/kg to LEO by mid-2030s; Starcloud cost parity ($0.05/kWh) contingent on Starship $500/kg. At $200/kg and ~15 kg/kW all-in (solar 5-10 kg/kW at 100-200 W/kg SOA + radiators 2-25 kg/kW + compute/structure ~5 kg/kW), launch adds only ~$3/W vs terrestrial datacenter capex $10-15/W — below ~$500/kg launch stops being the binding item; manufacturing throughput and 5-7-yr replacement cadence take over.

MASS GATING vs LAUNCH CAPACITY: ~15,000-50,000 t/GW-IT with conventional tech, maybe ~5,000 t/GW by 2035 with thin-film solar + advanced radiators. Global upmass 2024 ~1,500-2,000 t/yr (Starlink-dominated). Even at the WWII 2.5x/yr ceiling on upmass (2,000 -> ~78,000 t/yr by 2029), first orbital GW-IT lands ~2029-31 and multi-GW/yr relief only ~2032+ under aggressive assumptions.

DEBRIS/REGULATION: 43,000+ tracked objects >10 cm; ~1.2M modeled fragments 1-10 cm; ~14,000 active satellites (Feb 2026) vs 1.23M proposed across ITU/FCC filings; Starlink logged 144,404 avoidance maneuvers in H1-2025 alone; ESA 2026 Space Environment Report: +20% LEO collision probability, several bands past modeled Kessler threshold. SpaceX filed with FCC Jan 30 2026 for up to 1M satellites for space datacenters at 500-2,000 km (SPCX watch-position relevance: orbital compute is now explicitly in the SPCX bull case).

PROJECTS/TIMELINE: Starcloud-2 (Oct 2026, H100s in orbit; already ran Gemma + trained a model on Starcloud-1); Starcloud $170M Series A at $1.1B, whitepaper targets 5 GW with 4x4 km solar arrays — requires radiators ~32x better than ISS SOA; its 40 MW-per-single-Starship/$8.2M claim critiqued as needing ~22 launches. Google Suncatcher: 81-satellite clusters in 1-km radius, 1.6 Tbps optical inter-sat links, 2 prototype sats with Planet by early 2027. Starcloud ITU filing: 88,000-satellite compute constellation.
base_rates: Launch cost decline: ~20x over 30 yrs (Shuttle ~$65k/kg -> F9 ~$2,800/kg); Google assumes ~20% learning per doubling of cumulative mass — $200/kg by mid-2030s requires Starship full-reuse cadence with no gap years.
Space solar power / power-beaming architectures: ~50 years of studies (NASA/DOE 1970s onward), zero commercial deployments — base rate of beaming-dependent architectures shipping ≈ 0.
Megaconstellation execution: Starlink went 0 -> ~8,000 active sats and ~10,000+ t deployed in ~6 years — proof that 1,000s of t/yr of coordinated orbital mass deployment is achievable by one actor.

Space hardware advanced-concept maturation: TRL 4 -> flight at scale historically 8-15 yrs; liquid droplet radiators have sat at TRL 3-4 for 40 years — do not let the model buy 7x radiator mass improvement before ~2032.
LEO satellite service life 5-7 yrs (drag, radiation, obsolescence) — conveniently matches GPU depreciation; replacement flow ~15-20%/yr of orbital stock mass, permanently consuming launch capacity.

Orbital debris governance: no binding international debris rules exist; regulatory regimes historically clamp AFTER a salient accident (base rate from nuclear/aviation: one catastrophic event -> multi-year licensing freeze).
contested: '$200/kg by mid-2030s' — pure learning-curve extrapolation by an interested party (Google); Starship has not yet demonstrated full reusability economics. Model as distribution, median closer to $400-600/kg in 2033.
Starcloud's 40 MW per single Starship launch for $8.2M — independent analyses say ~22 launches; whitepaper's post-install energy cost of $0.002/kWh widely disputed.

Whether thermal is the dominant mass driver: 'thermal wall' analyses (7,000 t radiators/100 MW) vs Mach33's 'radiators are only 10-20% of mass at 100 kW' — resolution: both true; dominance grows with compute density and falls with radiator temperature. Contest is over the achievable operating point.
LDR 7x mass advantage — never flight-demonstrated; droplet evaporation/charging losses and pointing in formation-flying clusters unsolved.

Kessler status: ESA 2026 says several bands past threshold; a 'Kessler Syndrome Myth' skeptic literature calls the cascade timeline centuries-scale alarmism. The model should carry Kessler as a low-probability/high-impact shock, not a trend.

HBM sensitivity at 2 krad(Si): Google reports 'irregularities' not failures — whether this forces shielding mass/derating at scale or is fully masked by ECC is unresolved (single ground-beam test, n=1 vendor).

'5-10x more usable solar flux in space than best terrestrial sites' — true for W/m2-continuous (1,361 W/m2, ~99% duty in dawn-dusk SSO) but irrelevant if panels are cheap and land is not the terrestrial constraint; the real terrestrial constraint is grid interconnect, which space does bypass.

stocks: launch_upmass_t_per_yr (capacity stock; subject to existing WWII 2.5x/yr ceiling test; base ~2,000 t/yr in 2026)
orbital_energized_gw (space analog of energized-GW; NO 3-stage terrestrial pipeline — gated instead by upmass tonnage and specific-mass tech)
space_specific_mass_kg_per_kw (tech stock: starts ~20-30 kg/kW all-in 2026, floor ~4-6 kg/kW; radiator component floor ~1-2 kg/kW because AREA is T^4-fixed even when areal mass improves)
orbital_compute_stock (adds to compute_stock with 0.85-0.95 effectiveness multiplier for SEU/checkpoint + downlink overhead)
orbital_congestion_index (cumulative active sats + debris proxy; drives regulatory-drag and Kessler-shock hazard)
loops: R-launch-learning: upmass scale -> $/kg falls ~20%/cumulative doubling -> orbital deployment demand -> more upmass (reinforcing; capped by B-WWII)
B-WWII-ceiling: upmass growth capped at 2.5x/yr off established base (reuse existing mobilization test)
B-replacement-tax: orbital stock mass / 6-yr life = mandatory replacement upmass, crowding out net new deployment (balancing; bites hard once orbital stock is large)

B-congestion-clamp: congestion index -> avoidance costs + licensing drag -> deployment throttle; plus stochastic Kessler/collision shock (hazard rising in congestion) that freezes deployment 1-2 yrs via the existing shock module

B-power-rent-arbitrage (the key coupling to the binding constraint): terrestrial power rents high and persistent -> allocation share of upmass to orbital compute rises with 3-5 yr lag -> orbital GW relieves compute-power demand -> rents ease marginally. This is the ONLY endogenous relief valve for the never-normalizing power constraint, and it is tonnage-capped so relief is a trickle before ~2031-32.
couplings: orbital_energized_gw adds to power available FOR COMPUTE ONLY (bypasses grid/interconnect pipeline entirely; do not let it serve general demand — beaming to ground at 40-45% efficiency is uneconomic, so no space->grid flow)
orbital_compute_stock feeds the existing (compute x algo_eff)^0.85 aggregate with effectiveness ~0.9

gate: annual orbital_gw_added = allocated_upmass_t / (space_specific_mass_kg_per_kw x 1e6/GW-conversion); specific-mass improvement is a separate slow tech stock — NEVER let launch-$/kg decline reduce kg/kW (launch cost and radiator physics are orthogonal; only the $ penalty of mass falls with cheap launch)

SPCX watch position: SPCX revenue/valuation gains an orbital-compute option leg (FCC 1M-sat filing Jan 30 2026) driven by the same launch_upmass stock; a Kessler shock or congestion clamp hits both Starlink and orbital-compute legs simultaneously (correlated downside through the Dec-2026 lockup waterfall and beyond)
geopolitics layer: orbital assets are outside national grids but inside launch-site and spectrum jurisdictions — ITU/FCC licensing is a chokepoint a US-China shock can close

lessons_for_model: Space compute CANNOT materially relieve the power constraint inside the 2026-2036 window before ~2031-32: it is tonnage-gated, not capital-gated. Even at the 2.5x/yr WWII ceiling on upmass and optimistic 5,000-15,000 t/GW, cumulative orbital capacity by 2033 is single-digit GW vs terrestrial AI demand of 100+ GW. Model it as a late-window trickle relief valve, not a fix — consistent with power never normalizing endogenously in 95% of runs.

Separate the two constraint classes explicitly: SCALES AWAY with cheap launch = shielding mass, structure, solar array cost, replacement cadence cost. DOES NOT SCALE AWAY = radiator AREA (Stefan-Boltzmann T^4 at chip-compatible temps), spectrum/orbital-slot allocation, debris externality, beaming losses. Radiator MASS per watt is partially improvable (5-10 kg/m2 -> ~1-2 kg/m2 thin-film, LDR 7x claim) but its floor is a physics+TRL constraint on a ~decade timescale — keep kg/kW as its own tech stock with a hard floor.

Radiation is a solved-enough problem and should NOT be modeled as a constraint: COTS advanced-node silicon (Trillium at 15 krad, H100s flying on Starcloud) survives 5-yr LEO doses; encode as a ~0.9 effectiveness multiplier + 5-7 yr hardware life. The interesting consequence is the replacement-tax loop, not failure risk.

Power beaming to ground at ~40-45% end-to-end kills the 'space power for terrestrial compute' arbitrage — the model should have NO space->grid power flow. Space power is only monetizable through co-located orbital compute, which is why the SPCX/Starcloud/Suncatcher architectures all co-locate.

The economics flip below ~$500/kg launch: at $200/kg the launch cost of an orbital watt (~$3/W) undercuts terrestrial datacenter capex + 15-yr power rents. If the model's power rents persist as they do, orbital compute becomes NPV-positive around 2032-34 in the base case — implement the arbitrage loop so allocation responds endogenously to the rent level rather than by scenario switch.

Add a Kessler/regulatory clamp as a stochastic shock whose hazard rises with cumulative deployment (14k active sats now, 1.23M proposed, avoidance maneuvers doubling ~yearly): low annual probability (~1-3%) but it freezes the entire relief valve AND the SPCX position simultaneously — a correlated tail the trade book should price against the Dec-9-2026 lockup timeline.

For SPCX specifically: the Jan-30-2026 FCC filing for 1M compute satellites converts space-datacenters from narrative to filed intent; treat it as a real option on the launch_upmass stock rather than near-term revenue, and note it increases SPCX's beta to both power-rent persistence (upside) and debris regulation (downside).

briefs.topic: Space solar power (SBSP) as a power-relief channel vs orbital compute, plus the defense/mega-constellation launch demand floor and launch-demand elasticity to defense budgets, 2024-2026
key_numbers: SBSP demo scale (state of the art): Caltech SSPD-1/MAPLE (2023) first space-to-ground detection — milliwatt-scale received; JAXA OHISAMA (180 kg sat, 400 km LEO, 2 m^2 panel) transmitted ~1 kW at microwave from orbit 2025-26 to Suwa/Yokohama receivers — received energy at ground orders of magnitude below 1 kW (press conflates transmitted vs received)
ESA SOLARIS roadmap: demonstrator 2030, pilot plant 2035, commercial GW plant 2040 — i.e., zero grid-relevant SBSP inside the 2026-2036 model horizon even on ESA's own optimistic schedule

SBSP LCOE range: ESA-commissioned Frazer-Nash/London Economics EUR 88.5-155.5/MWh (2040 terms, assumes $300-500/kg launch); independent/NASA-side estimates ~$500/MWh best case vs <$50/MWh terrestrial solar+storage; NASA 2024 study: 12-80x terrestrial cost
Mass physics: 1 GW SBSP array ~10,000 tonnes to orbit; $60B lift bill at $6,000/kg, ~$5B at $500/kg; current Falcon 9 ~$2,700/kg, Starship target $200/kg, McKinsey competitiveness threshold ~$500/kg
China: CAST Bishan (Chongqing) 2-km ground verification array; orbital high-power test targeted 2028, first MW-scale plants ~2030, GW GEO ~2050 — schedule has slipped repeatedly
Aetherflux: $60M raised ($50M Series A — Index, Interlagos, BEV, a16z, NEA), IR-laser LEO constellation, first demo sat 2026, kW-class defense/remote-site niche (not grid relief)

Orbital compute: 1 GW orbital datacenter ~$42.4B, ~3x terrestrial equivalent; Starcloud $1.1B valuation (Mar 2026, $170M raise), 88,000-sat FCC filing, Starcloud-2 with H100/Blackwell Oct 2026; Google Suncatcher TPU v6e prototypes 2027; first multi-operator production workloads in orbit Feb 2026

Golden Dome: CBO $1.2T/20yr total; 7,800 space-based interceptors at ~$22M each, 5-yr service life implies ~1,600/yr replenishment (~30,000 sats over 20 yrs); SBIs at 300-500 km LEO; CBO assumes $500/kg launch; 12 SBI contractors named Apr 2026, $3.2B initial awards; FY27 request $17.5B (only $398M in base budget)
Space Force budget: FY26 $26.3B base + $13.8B reconciliation = ~$40B (+30%+ vs FY25 ~$29B); reconciliation lines: $5.6B space-based interceptors, $7.2B space sensors, $2B airborne-targeting sats

Defense launch line items: PWSA launches FY25 4 launches/$357M -> FY26 7 launches/$648M (+75% count, +81% dollars); NSSL Phase 3 Lane 2 (Apr 2025): $13.7B for ~54 missions 2027-32 (SpaceX $5.9B, ULA $5.4B, Blue Origin $2.4B), ~84 total NSSL-3 launches, roughly 2x Phase 2 spend; FY25 assignments SpaceX 7/$845.8M; FY26 SpaceX 5/$714M + ULA 2/$428M

Mega-constellation floor: SpaceX 165 orbital launches in 2025 (record), ~140-160 forecast 2026; Starlink $10-11.4B revenue (61-67% of SpaceX total, 63% EBITDA margin), 9,500+ sats; Amazon Kuiper: FCC deadline 1,618 sats by Jul 2026, 80+ launches procured across 5 vehicles (Vulcan 38, Ariane 6 18, F9 13+, New Glenn 12+, Atlas V 9) — largest commercial launch procurement ever, 20+ launches 2026 / 30+ 2027; China Guowang ~190 sats by mid-2026 (target 310 by year-end, of 13,000), Qianfan 162 by May 2026 after a 2025 pause (thruster/gyro failures)

Implied launch-demand elasticity to defense budget 2024-2026: DoD topline +~13% (with reconciliation) while Space Force +30-38% and launch-specific lines +75-81% -> arc elasticity roughly 3-6, but driven by one-shot reconciliation money
base_rates: SBSP has been perpetually 15-20 years away since the 1978 DOE/NASA reference system; every GW-scale roadmap for ~50 years has slipped; demos remain mW-kW received scale — base rate of grid-relevant SBSP arriving within any given decade: near zero (<5% for pre-2036)

Launch cost declines: Falcon 9 cut $/kg roughly 10x over ~15 years; SBSP and orbital compute both require another ~5-10x (to $200-500/kg) — one full additional learning-curve generation, historically a 10-15 yr process

Constellation replenishment: 5-yr LEO satellite life means ~20%/yr steady-state replacement — launch demand from deployed constellations is recurring, not one-time (Starlink already demonstrates this)

Mega-project deployment speed: Starlink went 0 -> 9,500+ sats in ~7 years, the fastest space deployment ever; Golden Dome's 7,800 SBIs by early 2030s assumes matching or beating that with a first-of-kind weapon system

Defense supplemental/reconciliation funding historically mean-reverts: one-shot bills produce spend pulses, not sustained slope changes — lawmakers and industry already flag FY26 reconciliation as non-recurring
National-security launch spend roughly doubles per NSSL phase (~5-6 yr cycle), a durable ~12-15%/yr trend growth independent of AI capex
contested: JAXA OHISAMA '1 kW beamed to ground' headlines: 1 kW is transmitted power; power actually received at ground receivers was orders of magnitude lower — press-level conflation, treat received-power milestone as still kW-scale-transmitted/mW-scale-received

SBSP LCOE: ESA-commissioned EUR 88.5-155/MWh vs independent ~$500/MWh and NASA's 12-80x terrestrial finding — advocates' numbers assume $300-500/kg launch, in-space assembly at scale, and 30+ yr array life, none demonstrated
China 2028 orbital test / 2030 MW-scale plant claims — repeatedly slipped; aspirational, not funded-program milestones
CBO Golden Dome assumptions: $22M per interceptor and $500/kg launch are both unproven; administration counterclaim of ~$175B total vs CBO $1.2T is a 7x disagreement
Golden Dome funding durability: FY27 $17.5B request has only $398M in base budget — the rest requires a future reconciliation bill; the launch-demand floor from Golden Dome is politically contingent

Starcloud 88,000-satellite filing and 'orbital datacenters relieve the power constraint' narrative: single-analysis $42.4B/GW (~3x terrestrial) figure; thermal radiator mass, radiation-induced hardware life (~5 yr), and downlink bandwidth are unresolved; McKinsey $500/kg threshold is a modeling assumption, not observed
SpaceX 2026 cadence forecasts range 140-179 (Polymarket) vs 160 (analyst) — Starship transition risk cuts both ways

stocks: launch_capacity_tons_per_year (new stock): mass-to-orbit capacity with its own learning curve; grows with cumulative launches, funded by max(defense, constellation, AI) demand — NOT by AI capex alone
launch_cost_per_kg (state variable / inverse-learning stock): declines with cumulative tonnage; gates both orbital_compute and any SBSP channel; currently ~$2,700/kg, thresholds at $500 and $200

orbital_compute_stock (GW-equivalent): small side-stock feeding compute_stock with ~2.5-3x cost multiplier, 5-yr depreciation (radiation life), capped at low-single-digit % of total compute through 2033
defense_constellation_stock (satellites on orbit): Golden Dome + PWSA + allied constellations; 5-yr life -> 20%/yr replenishment outflow that sustains launch demand endogenously
sbsp_capacity_gw: legitimate to include but initialize ~0 and expect median run to keep it ~0 through 2036; treat as post-horizon option, not a relief valve
loops: R (defense-funded launch learning): defense budget -> NSSL/Golden Dome/PWSA launch contracts -> cadence -> cumulative tonnage -> $/kg down -> more missions affordable -> more contracts. This loop runs even in AI-bust scenarios — it is the decoupling mechanism between launch learning and the AI capex cycle

B (power scarcity -> SBSP hope valve, DOES NOT CLOSE in horizon): power rents -> SBSP investment -> 8-15 yr pipeline + aperture physics + $/kg gate -> negligible GW before 2036. Model explicitly as a non-functioning balancing loop so the power constraint stays binding, matching the existing 95%-of-runs finding

B (orbital compute bypass, weak): ground power rents -> orbital compute investment -> gated on launch_cost_per_kg < ~$500 AND thermal/radiation maturity -> small addition to compute_stock at 3x cost. Opens partially ~2030-2033 in optimistic launch branches only

R (constellation replenishment): deployed sats -> 20%/yr replacement demand -> sustained cadence -> lower $/kg -> bigger economical constellations. Recurring-demand ratchet that puts a floor under cadence independent of new programs
couplings: launch demand = defense floor + constellation replenishment + AI/orbital-compute marginal demand; defense floor scales with defense budget at short-run elasticity ~3-6 but implemented as a reconciliation PULSE (2025-2027) decaying toward NSSL trend growth (~12-15%/yr), not a permanent slope

SBSP relief channel gated on BOTH launch_cost_per_kg crossing ~$300-500 AND an 8-12 yr construction pipeline — strictly longer than the existing 3-yr terrestrial power pipeline, so it can never outrun it within the horizon

orbital_compute feeds the existing (compute x algo_eff)^0.85 production function but with a cost-of-capital penalty ~3x and hard share cap; its 5-yr life makes it a high-churn stock (contrast 15-yr power rents duration)

WWII 2.5x/yr mobilization ceiling: apply to launch TONNAGE not launch count — Starship (~100 t/flight vs F9 ~17 t) lets tonnage grow 1.5-2.5x/yr off the 2025 base (165 launches) while launch count grows only ~1.1-1.3x/yr; tonnage can plausibly run near the ceiling, unlike energized-GW

SPCX watch position coupling: Starlink = 61-67% of revenue at 63% EBITDA margin plus a defense-funded launch floor (NSSL $13.7B, Golden Dome awards) -> SPCX cash flows are substantially insulated from an AI-datacenter bust; downside correlation to AI cycle lower than market narrative implies through the Dec 9 2026 lockup waterfall

lessons_for_model: Do NOT add SBSP as an endogenous power-relief channel for 2026-2036: demos are mW-received to 1-kW-transmitted scale, best-case roadmaps (ESA) put pilot plants at 2035 and commercial GW at 2040, and LCOE is 2-10x terrestrial even at $500/kg launch. This VALIDATES the existing finding that power never normalizes endogenously — SBSP is the most-cited escape hatch and it is closed within the horizon

Add a launch-learning stock decoupled from AI capex: defense (NSSL 84 missions/$13.7B 2027-32, Golden Dome ~1,600 sats/yr replenishment) plus mega-constellations (Kuiper 80+ procured launches, Guowang/Qianfan monthly cadence, Starlink replacement) guarantee $/kg keeps falling in ALL scenarios including AI-bust branches — this changes the state of the world the model exits 2036 into, even if it never relieves power in-horizon

Orbital compute is a marginal valve, not a structural one: gate on $/kg < $500, apply ~3x cost multiplier and low-single-digit share cap on compute_stock, 5-yr hardware life; binding sub-constraints are thermal radiator mass, radiation, and downlink — not power. Median contribution to power relief pre-2033: ~0. Optimistic Starship branch: a few % of compute by 2034-2036

Model defense launch elasticity as an asymmetric pulse: observed 2024-2026 arc elasticity ~3-6 (launch lines +75-81% on +13% topline) is reconciliation-driven one-shot money; encode a 2025-2027 pulse decaying to NSSL trend (~2x per 5-6 yr phase, ~13%/yr), with a political-continuation Bernoulli on Golden Dome out-year funding (FY27 is 98% reconciliation-dependent)

Apply the 2.5x WWII ceiling to launch tonnage, where it can actually bind: Starship's per-flight mass step means tonnage (not launch count) is the fast variable — launch tonnage is one of the few stocks in the whole model that can legitimately run at or near the mobilization ceiling off an established base

Replenishment turns launch demand into a stock-with-outflow, not a project: 5-yr LEO life = 20%/yr replacement across Starlink (9,500+), Kuiper (3,200+), Guowang/Qianfan (25,000+ planned), Golden Dome (7,800) — by 2030 replacement demand alone exceeds today's total launch market; this is the durable cadence floor

For the SPCX watch position: the defense floor plus Starlink margin structure argue SPCX is a launch-learning/defense play more than an AI-cycle play; the $1.77T->$1.52T post-IPO drawdown into the Dec 2026 lockup waterfall prices AI-correlation that the revenue mix (61-67% Starlink, growing NSSL share) does not fully support — but Golden Dome funding fragility is the offsetting contested risk

# Space Module Spec — `space.rs` for `singularity-econ`

**Verdict on the one question:** Orbital compute does **not** relax the terrestrial power constraint inside 2026–2036. It is tonnage-gated, not capital-gated: 1 GW-IT in orbit costs 10,000–30,000 t to LEO (10–30 kg/kW) against a 2026 world launch base of ~3,500–4,000 t/yr. Even growing at the model's own 2.5x/yr WWII ceiling *after* a Starship full-reuse proof (Bernoulli, p≈0.6–0.75 by end-2027), cumulative orbital GW-equiv stays <1 GW before ~2031 and reaches central 1–3 GW (bull 8–12) by 2033–2036, versus a terrestrial `ai_power` path in the hundreds of GW. The module's honest output is a **2034–2036 tail rent-clipper** (shaves `power_margin` excess 10–25% in the bull branch, ~0 in central) plus a long-run ceiling on power rents — it must leave the "power binds ≥6/11 years, never normalizes endogenously" result intact. The two gating thresholds: **launch price < breakeven_$/kg = 200 + 300×power_rent_index** (i.e. $200/kg vs unconstrained terrestrial per Google Suncatcher, ~$500/kg vs 2026-level queue rents per McKinsey/Starcloud — the model's own power rents endogenously widen the gate), and **kg_per_kw < ~20** (radiator+solar specific mass, which does NOT improve with cheap launch — Stefan-Boltzmann area at chip temps is launch-cost-orthogonal).

---

## 1. Stocks (5, plus one Pipeline)

Add `pub mod space;` with `SpaceParams`, `SpaceState`. All fields f64, annual step, same idiom as robotics.

```rust
pub struct SpaceState {
    pub cum_upmass_t: f64,        // Wright-law state. init 28_000.0 (cumulative kg-to-orbit since 2000, McDowell payload-mass series)
    pub launch_capacity_tpy: f64, // init 4_000.0 (2025 realized 3,193 t + trend)
    pub launch_cost_per_kg: f64,  // COST, init 2_000.0; derived from cum_upmass each year
    pub kg_per_kw: f64,           // specific-mass tech stock, init 40.0, floor 8.0
    pub orbital_gw_it: f64,       // energized GW-IT in orbit, init ~0.0 (2e-5)
    pub orbital_pipe: Pipeline,   // 2 stages (design/manifest → commission), init flow 0.0
    pub starship_proven: bool,    // Bernoulli drawn in MC harness, like incident_year
    pub second_supplier: bool,    // rent-wedge collapse Bernoulli
}
```

**Per-year step (call between the R4 block and the constraints block in `simulate`):**

```text
1. kg_per_kw *= (1 - specific_mass_decline);  kg_per_kw = kg_per_kw.max(kg_per_kw_floor)
2. launch_cost_per_kg = cost_2026 * (cum_upmass_t / 28_000).powf((1.0 - wright_lr).log2())   // Wright on cumulative mass
   price = launch_cost_per_kg * rent_wedge   // wedge 1.8 → 1.15 once second_supplier (SpaceX internal deployment pays wedge 1.2)
3. growth = if starship_proven { launch_growth_fast } else { launch_growth_slow };
   growth = growth.min(reg_cadence_ceiling(year));            // 0.6/yr pre-2029, 1.5 after (FAA lag)
   launch_capacity_tpy *= (1.0 + growth).min(2.5);            // WWII ceiling, hard
4. upmass = launch_capacity_tpy * 0.9;  cum_upmass_t += upmass
5. replacement_t = orbital_gw_it * kg_per_kw * 1000.0 * orbital_attrition   // B-replacement tax
   available_t = (upmass * (1.0 - preempt_share) - replacement_t).max(0.0)  // Starlink+defense pre-empt
6. power_rent_index = ((power_margin - normal_margin) / (margin_ceiling - normal_margin)).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
   breakeven = 200.0 + 300.0 * power_rent_index               // THE coupling to existing rent machinery
   gate = logistic((breakeven - price) / 50.0)                // soft economic gate
   allocated_t = available_t * gate
7. delivered_gw = orbital_pipe.step(allocated_t / (kg_per_kw * 1000.0))     // t → GW; 2-yr material delay; NO step_accel — launch cadence is regulatory/physical, ASI doesn't compress FAA reviews (defensible either way; keep it conservative)
8. orbital_gw_it = orbital_gw_it * (1.0 - orbital_attrition) + delivered_gw
9. orbital_gw_equiv = orbital_gw_it * orbital_effectiveness   // 0.60 penalty stack
```

Two regimes for growth (the 2016-2019 flat / 2019-2025 42%/yr lesson): `launch_growth_slow = 0.12`, `launch_growth_fast = 0.35`. `starship_proven` flips via MC draw p=0.7 by end-2027 (as of Jul 2026 Starship has never completed full orbital insertion — the gate is live, not formality).

## 2. Coupling into the power bottleneck

Exactly two lines change in `simulate()` — orbital GW-equiv relaxes **only** the power cap; chips, capital, and demand gates are untouched, so orbital compute units still consume silicon and capex through the existing machinery (this is the physics-honest structure for free):

```rust
// line ~734: power_headroom
let eff_power = ai_power + space.orbital_gw_equiv;   // was: ai_power
let power_headroom = (eff_power + power_additions - compute_stock * gw_per_unit).max(0.0);
// line ~779: power_utilization denominator
let power_utilization = (power_demand_gw / (ai_power + space.orbital_gw_equiv).max(1e-9)).min(1.35);
```

**Penalty structure** (`orbital_effectiveness = 0.60`): 0.95 availability (solar events) × 0.70 workload addressability (training + batch inference only; real-time inference can't fly; ground↔orbit multi-Tbps ingress undemonstrated) × 0.90 SEU/ECC/checkpoint + downlink overhead. Radiation is deliberately NOT a failure channel — it's solved-enough (Trillium 15 krad, H100s flying); it lives in the 5–6 yr life (`orbital_attrition = 0.18`) instead, which is the buried killer: whole-stack consumable vs 15-yr terrestrial facility. **No space→grid flow ever** — power beaming is ~40–45% end-to-end; orbital power is monetizable only through co-located compute.

Loop registry: **R5** (Wright launch learning: upmass → doublings → $/kg ↓ → gate opens → more upmass) with gain `r5_launch_learning` in `Loops`; **B11** (power-rent arbitrage: rents ↑ → breakeven ↑ → gate opens → orbital GW → rents ease — the model's only endogenous power relief, sized to a trickle); **B12** (replacement tax: stock × 18%/yr × kg/kW permanently consumes capacity). Setting `r5 = 0.0` and `orbital_effectiveness = 0.0` must exactly recover golden vectors.

## 3. Parameters and justification

| Param | Default | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| `cum_upmass_2026_t` | 28,000 | McDowell payload-mass series (pick ONE series; 16,185 t in orbit end-2025 + pre-2015 cumulative) |
| `launch_capacity_2026_tpy` | 4,000 | 2025 realized 3,193 t, 28%/yr trend |
| `wright_lr` | 0.212 | PNAS Nexus 2026 experience curve, 21.2%/doubling — on COST, not price |
| `rent_wedge` | 1.8 → 1.15 | F9 list price flat 2016–2026 while cost fell (monopoly); symmetric with power-rents mechanic. Second-supplier Bernoulli p≈0.35 by 2031 (New Glenn / Zhuque-3 heavy) |
| `launch_cost_2026` | $2,000/kg | F9 ~$2,700 reused price, Starship realized ~$2,500 at 40 t; cost basis lower |
| `kg_per_kw` init / floor | 40 / 8 | Independent engineering 34–59 kg/kW today; floor = radiator ~2 (T⁴ area floor at 50–80°C) + solar ~4 + compute/structure ~2. SpaceX's 10 kg/kW claim lives only in the MC bull tail (sample log-uniform [10, 60]) |
| `specific_mass_decline` | 0.15/yr | 85→10–15 kg/kW over ~decade per Starcloud/Suncatcher roadmaps, TRL-honest (LDR stuck at TRL 3-4 for 40 yrs — no 7x jumps before 2032) |
| `preempt_share` | 0.65 | Starlink replacement (20%/yr of 9,500+ sats), Kuiper, NSSL/Golden Dome floor — recurring demand, launcher's own payloads were 85% of 2019-25 growth |
| `orbital_attrition` | 0.18 | 5–6 yr whole-stack LEO life (drag, radiation, coating degradation) |
| `orbital_effectiveness` | 0.60 | penalty stack above |
| `p_starship_by_2027` | 0.70 | 13 flights, zero full orbital insertions, July 2026 booster loss; schedule-slip base rate 3–5 yr |
| MC ranges | — | tonnes/yr 2030: bear 8k / central 15–25k / bull 60k; orbital GW 2033: 0.3 / 1–3 / 8–12; $/kg cost 2030: $400–700 |

## 4. Validation contract (falsifiable, add to `tests/backtest.rs`)

1. **WWII ceiling on launch tonnage**: add `(launch_capacity_tpy, floor 500.0)` to the ratio list in `no_stock_outruns_wwii_mobilization_ceiling`. Domain evidence the ceiling is right: 70 years of spaceflight max is 1.72x/yr global (2023-24), 1.97x single-program (F9 2021-22) — nothing has ever violated 2.5x. Launch tonnage is the one stock that can legitimately *approach* the ceiling (Starship per-flight mass step).
2. **Backcast 2016→2025**: initialized at 338 t/yr and slow-regime growth, flipping to fast-regime in 2019 (Starlink self-demand proxy), the module must land 2025 upmass in [2,200, 4,500] t and cost in [$1,500, $3,500]/kg. Falsifies the two-regime + Wright structure jointly.
3. **Tonnage binds before economics**: in ≥90% of MC draws, `orbital_gw_equiv < 1.0` before 2031 even when the price gate is forced fully open (`gate = 1.0`). If economics ever binds first pre-2031, the mass budget is mis-specified.
4. **Headline result survives**: with the module on at defaults, `Binding::Power` still ≥6 of 11 years (existing test unchanged), and 2036 `power_margin` reduction vs module-off is ≤25% of the excess over `normal_margin` — and exactly 0 in draws where `starship_proven` never fires.
5. **Physics floor**: delivered GW per allocated tonne never exceeds 1/(8,000 t/GW) in any draw (kg_per_kw floor 8) — catches any accidental coupling of kg/kW to launch cost, which are orthogonal.
6. **Ablation parity**: `r5_launch_learning = 0` + `orbital_effectiveness = 0` reproduces golden vectors bit-for-bit (regression guard, same pattern as `geo_shocks: Vec::new()`).

## 5. What NOT to model

- **SBSP / power beaming to ground** — no space→grid flow, period. 50 years of studies, mW-received demos, ESA's own roadmap says commercial GW 2040. Its absence *is* the finding that power never normalizes.
- **Kessler / debris as a trend** — at most a `GeoShock` variant (1–3%/yr hazard, freezes deployment 1–2 yr, correlated SPCX downside); skip in v1.
- **Launch counts, vehicles, sites** — tonnage only (counts grew 16%/yr vs mass 28%/yr; counts mislead).
- **Radiation as failure risk** — folded into attrition + effectiveness. Keep a 20% MC branch where fleet-scale HBM failures push attrition to 0.30.
- **China space stack** — lags US 4–6 yrs on reusable heavy-lift (10% of world mass on 28% of flights); immaterial in-horizon.
- **Orbital latency/market microstructure, insurance, robotic servicing** — servicing is optionally one Bernoulli (life 5→10 yr post-2032, bull tail only).
- **Every SpaceX narrative number** — 1M t/yr (300x world upmass), 100 kW/t, $10–20/kg, 1M-sat FCC filing (<10% of filed sats ever fly). Default to independent numbers; company claims live only in the bull tail.

## 6. SPCX book implications

- The orbital-compute leg of the $1.50T mark ($114, below the $135 offer, −50% from ATH) is a **real but 2033+ call option** — this module prices it as tonnage-gated optionality, not terminal value. Any bank model showing orbital GW relieving power pre-2031 is falsified by test #3's mass budget.
- **Picks-and-shovels asymmetry**: SpaceX gets paid (Google Suncatcher launches, Starcloud manifests) whether or not orbital DCs pencil; the rent wedge means SpaceX-internal deployment crosses the gate ~2 yrs before third parties. Upside concentrates in SPCX; the RKLB/rad-hard basket is a 5–10% capex skim at best (Neutron 13 t is not DC tonnage; NVIDIA's commercial-node rad-tolerance kills the rad-hard-prime moat).
- **Binary to watch before the lockup waterfall**: full orbital insertion + booster recovery before the final Dec 8 2026 release (book says Dec 9 — fix). Waterfall supply peaks Aug–Nov (20% + 7% tranches + ~28% Q3-earnings release); the better entry is the Oct/Nov tranche, Dec 8 is likely anticlimax. F13 (sats deployed, booster lost) ≈ valuation-neutral.
